title: A Little Bit of Problem-Solving in Every Lesson
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton gives ten practical tips for embedding one short, unfamiliar problem in every maths lesson, as a follow-up to his account of doing this with a whole department. The argument is that problem-solving only becomes routine when the teacher prepares for it as carefully as for any other part of the lesson. He moves from sourcing good problems, to solving them as a mathematician first, to then asking how a struggling or finished student would be supported or challenged. The delivery moves are low-stakes framing, thirty seconds of silent thinking, mini-whiteboards and the 4-2 solo-then-pair cycle. He closes with ways to choose which pairs to hear from and to showcase student work. It is a usable checklist for a teacher or department starting out with problem-solving.
points: Do the problem yourself first, then switch to the teacher hat and plan how you would support the stuck and extend the finished.
Because unfamiliar problems trigger fear of failure, the pitch (low stakes, effort matters, I believe you can) is part of the task design.
Thirty seconds of no talking and no writing prevents the instant 'I don't get it' and the dive into the first idea.
Mini-whiteboards plus the 4-2 cycle (4 minutes solo, 2 minutes with a partner) combine independent thinking with collaboration.
Targeted hand-up prompts and showcasing student work let the teacher pick which pairs to hear from and build a path to the solution.
quotes: It is only when we sit down and do a problem that we notice fun twists and turns, can predict where our students might struggle, or get inspired to think of variations and extensions. If doing this in a departmental meeting, I would recommend 5 minutes working on a problem on your own, and then 5 minutes sharing where you have got to with a colleague.

I have arrived at many lessons excited to share a problem with my students, only to find that my students struggled, finished early, or simply did not enjoy it. The mistake I made was not pausing to think about how to help my students get the most out of the problem.

Time files in lessons, and if we are not careful, we will not leave ourselves sufficient time to get the most out of the problem. Setting an alarm on my phone helps remind me to get cracking with the problem.
Students find unfamiliar problems challenging, and thus may be reluctant to engage with them for fear of failure. So, how we introduce the problem is important.
I am sold on this approach after trying it a few times. No speaking stops the inevitable I don’t get it. No writing stops students from diving straight in, forcing them to pause and think.
Mini-whiteboards are the ideal vehicle to tackle unfamiliar problems. Students have less fear about writing their ideas down as they can be rubbed away if needed.

You want students to work independently on a problem, but also to reap the benefits of collaboration. I find the 4-2 approach works well here, with students spending 4 minutes working on their own to see how far they can get, and then having 2 minutes to collaborate with their partner to compare progress and approaches.
